name: Moral luck
statement: People blame a careless act more heavily when it happens to cause harm, though the risk taken and the state of mind were the same either way.
meaning: Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel named a conflict inside ethics. Moral assessment is meant to track what an agent controls, and ordinary judgement tracks how things turned out. Nagel's own driver has had too much to drink and his car swerves on to the pavement. Whether a pedestrian is standing there is not up to him, yet it decides whether he is prosecuted for manslaughter. Psychology asks a different question from the one the philosophers asked. It asks whether outcome does move people's judgements, which kind of judgement it moves, and when the gap between the lucky and the unlucky agent opens or closes. The answers turn out to depend heavily on the measure used and on whether a participant sees one case or both.

origin.note: A two-paper symposium under the shared title 'Moral Luck' in volume 50. Williams runs from page 115 to page 135 and Nagel from page 137 to page 151, as the scanned symposium itself shows. Crossref and the publisher give the joint range as 115 to 152. The papers set the problem for later philosophy and supplied the label that the experimental work borrowed.

evidence: Fiery Cushman ran the comparison in 2008. He crossed what an agent believed, what the agent wanted and what actually happened, giving eight combinations across eight scenario contexts and 64 vignettes, with 160 people per condition and seven-point scales. For judgements of wrongness, belief explained 62% of the within-context variability, desire 21%, and the consequence 3%. For blame the consequence explained 22%. Permissibility behaved like wrongness at 3%, punishment like blame at 20%. Outcome moved blame and punishment and barely touched whether the act counted as wrong. Markus Kneer and Izabela Skoczen later ran ten preregistered experiments on 2,043 people. Their farmer, Ms Russel, spends the flood budget on refurbishing her workers' kitchens, and the season either passes quietly or the lodgings flood and a worker and his two children die. In the first experiment, which compared separate groups, the harmful ending raised blame by d = 0.70 and deserved punishment by d = 1.18.

replication.headline: The outcome effect on blame holds when different people see different endings, and shrinks when one person sees both, where most participants rate the two agents alike.
replication.detail: Kneer and Machery put the lucky and the unlucky agent in front of the same participants. Among the 95 people analysed in that study, 87% rated the two as equally blameworthy, 89% rated the acts equally wrong and 96% rated them equally permissible. For punishment the figure fell to 64%. Comparing separate groups, outcome moved all four judgements, and the effect ran through ascriptions of negligence, which ran in turn through differing estimates of how likely the harm had been. Kneer and Skoczen reproduce the shape of that result in 84 people who saw both endings side by side. Blame falls from d = 0.70 between subjects to d = 0.49 within subjects, and punishment from d = 1.18 to d = 0.63, both still significant. Aurore Gaboriaud and colleagues then adapted Cushman's scenarios to a mouse-tracking task run within participants, analysing 144 of the 145 they recruited. Outcome mattered, d = 0.53, and causal involvement weighed more on blame than on wrongness, p = .042. The outcome-by-judgement-type interaction that Cushman's dissociation predicts did not reach significance, p = .105.

study.cite: Gaboriaud, A., Gautheron, F., Quinton, J.-C., & Smeding, A. (2024). Wrongness and blame judgments and their dynamics: Toward a three-input processing model of moral judgment. International Review of Social Psychology, 37(1), 19.

limits: Cushman's percentages are shares of within-context variability from an analysis that treats each scenario context as a single case, which is how his paper describes the method. They are not standardised effect sizes and do not convert into a d, so they cannot be lined up against the figures beside them. The Kneer and Skoczen effect sizes here come from the published Cognition article, and the authors' PsyArXiv draft prints the same four numbers. No multi-site replication was located. Searches on 21 September 2026 of Crossref, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, the Psychological Science Accelerator's project list and the Collaborative Replications and Education Project site returned no moral-luck protocol. Three student class replications of Kneer and Machery's within-subjects study are registered on the Open Science Framework, at Texas Woman's University and at Brigham Young University-Idaho, and no published report of any of them was found. Kneer and Machery's own reference list promises 'Moral luck across cultures' with Stich, Rose and others as in preparation, and Crossref held no published version of it on that date.
misreadings: The philosophical claim and the psychological finding are separate claims. Philosophy asks whether outcome ought to bear on blame; the experiments record that it does, which leaves the ought untouched. A vote of the folk does not settle an ethical question, and Kneer and Machery's finding that most people equalise their judgements is not a proof that equalising is right. Their result is also read as showing the effect is an artefact of how blame is elicited. That is not what they report. They treat the between-subjects effect as real and explain it through negligence and probability ascriptions, and they find punishment stays outcome-sensitive even when the two cases sit side by side. The pair of drunk drivers who hit a tree and a child are Cushman's opening illustration rather than his stimulus. He uses them to contrast a $250 fine in Massachusetts with a sentence of two and a half to fifteen years for vehicular manslaughter, then tests welding, dentistry and carnival scenarios instead. Entry 195 covers outcome bias, where the judgement is of a decision taken under stated odds, and entry 48 covers hindsight bias, the mechanism Kneer and Skoczen invoke. The three bodies of evidence answer different questions and should not be pooled.
